newsitem.title: USA: U.S. labor leaders demand Herman hearings.
newsitem.headline: U.S. labor leaders demand Herman hearings.

text.p: America's major federation of trade unions on Wednesday stepped into the debate over the troubled nomination of Alexis Herman as Secretary of Labour, demanding the Senate hold hearings on the issue immediately.

Herman's nomination by President Clinton has been mired in the controversy surrounding the Democratic National Committee's fundraising efforts and no Senate hearings have yet been set to consider her cabinet position.
John Sweeney, president of the AFL-CIO, said in a statement the nomination hearings should go ahead immediately.
"It is time for Alexis Herman to be able to stand in an open forum and have her nomination considered by the United States Senate," he said.
Herman, who headed the White House Office of Public Liaison before her nomination, has been criticised by Republicans for her involvement in White House coffee meetings organised by the DNC.

She has been cited in particular for her role in helping set up a DNC-sponsored meeting last year involving Clinton and some of America's leading bankers, as well as federal banking regulator Eugene Ludwig.
Clinton has admitted it was a mistake for Ludwig to attend, and Herman said she decided not to go to the meeting when she found out DNC officials would be there.

Republican senators have also said Herman, who is black, may have violated a law barring certain government officials from engaging in political work when she helped recruit black donors for the Democrats.
Defending Herman, Sweeney told reporters, "It is unfair to working families to have the principal federal government department responsible for worker protection to be singled out and held hostage."

He said the AFL-CIO was impressed by Herman's "commitment to a working families agenda and her superb ability to advance such an agenda," adding that when the Senate confirmation hearings took place, "America's working families and their unions will be standing right beside her."
Meanwhile, Sweeney and his top aides Wednesday outlined their strategy for dealing with corporate America, including targeting multinational companies.

Sweeney announced the establishment of a new section of the federation, a department of corporate affairs, which would support corporations friendly to labour unions and attack those considered to be anti-labour.

The head of the new department, economist Ron Blackwell, told reporters at a news conference his section wanted to try and bring all employers into a "marriage" with the unions that would benefit both corporate and labour ideals.

"We basically want to see our employers succeed in whatever they do in the private sector or the public sector," her said. "But we want to see them succeed without benefit just to the owners and the chief executives, we want the employees to share in that prosperity, we want the communities in which they operate to share in that prosperity."
One of the new department's first tasks, Blackwell said, would be to distinguish the "high road" companies from the "low road" firms.
He described the "high road companies" as those which "produce quality products, serve customers well and reduce their prices by increasing the productivity of workers."
"Low road" companies, on the other hand, "only focus on price in the same tired way and try to compete successfully at the expense of their employees."
